review.material: The full public Springer abstract was read.
review.limitations: The complete paper, participant counts, statistical tests and measurement protocol were not inspected. Later sleeve studies were not substituted for this 2019 study.

evidence.description: Primary abstract for this particular conference paper.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: The authors develop a wearable sleeve that creates rhythmic warmth and slight pressure along the arm. They study whether its haptic pace relates to breathing and perceived calmness.

sections.title: Premise
sections.text: Material behaviour may provide affective feedback: a wearable’s physical action could influence bodily rhythm and experience.

sections.title: Method reported
sections.text: A controlled pilot compares haptic pacing with relaxed breathing pace and a pace 25% faster. Quantitative breathing observations are considered alongside qualitative self-reports.

sections.title: Reported outcome
sections.text: The abstract associates faster haptic action with faster breathing. Self-reports relate slower action to greater calmness and faster action to less calmness.

sections.title: What this does not establish
sections.text: The abstract omits the full sample and statistical detail. These preliminary associations do not establish treatment effectiveness, lasting anxiety reduction or suitability for every wearer.

sections.title: What to look for in the paper
sections.text: Separate physiological measurements from subjective reports and clinical outcomes. The material interface is a design-research case, not a medical recommendation.

terms.meaning: Physical sensations delivered through touch, here warmth and slight pressure.
An initial, limited investigation that informs further testing.
